Scouse is the distinctive accent and dialect of Liverpool, England, characterized by strong nasalization, unique vowel shifts, and a rising intonation pattern. It carries powerful working-class and urban identity and has become internationally recognized through Liverpool's cultural export and The Beatles, who were Scouse speakers.

Nasalized vowels give Scouse a distinctive nasal quality, particularly before ng sounds and throughout speech. The vowel shifts are distinctive, with the "face" vowel pronounced more openly, closer to the "trap" vowel, and "goat" becoming more front-rounded.

Intonation rises toward the end of statements, giving even declarative sentences a questioning tone. Questions rise even more steeply. Rhoticity, or the pronunciation of r, varies in Scouse. Traditionally Scouse was non-rhotic, but younger speakers are becoming more rhotic.

There is a merger of the th and f sounds in some words. The word "three" may become "free" and "thin" becomes "fin," though this is not consistent across all contexts.

Strong local pride and identity are central to Scouse culture. The accent is frequently featured in British media and comedy and is globally recognized through The Beatles and Liverpool's broader cultural influence. Like Scottish English, Scouse has another regionally distinct accent with strong community identity and non-standard grammar. Geordie, the Northeast accent, is similarly regionally distinctive and working-class marked. Cockney, the East London working-class accent, shares some phonological features and class associations with Scouse as well.
